BrickLink SOS Part 2

Piece Pavilion · November 6, 2026 · 8 min read

NONE OF THESE ANSWERS ARE COMPLETE YET. BrickLink has given the community a clearer update, but the cause of the disruption, a firm reopening time, and the effects on individual orders and inventory still need answers.

November 6, 2026 update. BrickLink's main website was checked again at approximately 6:31 a.m. Eastern (11:31 UTC) and redirected to its maintenance page. The two screenshots below were supplied for this report. They record the notices shown, not a live service-status feed.

BrickLink SOS continues. Since our first report, the message facing buyers and sellers has become more specific. There is a new maintenance screen, and the supplied Instagram Story from BrickLink gives a date alongside the expected waiting window: November 6.

That is useful progress in the communication. It gives people something concrete to plan around. It does not yet give a complete explanation of what happened, and it does not promise that the marketplace will reopen at the first time listed. For anyone with orders to pack, parts to buy, or inventory to reconcile, that distinction matters.

What BrickLink said on Instagram

The Instagram screenshot supplied for this update shows a Story from the verified bricklink account. Its heading reads, “BrickLink® is temporarily unavailable.” The statement then says:

“BrickLink is currently offline while our teams carry out necessary work. We expect the site to remain unavailable until at least 9:00 AM PST / 6:00 PM CET, Nov 6.

We're sorry for the disruption and appreciate your patience while we complete this work.”

The supplied image lets readers see the actual wording rather than rely on a secondhand description. The Story says the site is offline and that teams are carrying out necessary work. It does not say that nothing is wrong, identify a specific technical fault, or announce that service has already returned.

It is also worth keeping the format clear: the image is a screenshot of an Instagram Story, not a newly verified permanent feed post. We have reproduced the supplied screenshot and attributed the statement to the account shown in it. We are not assigning a precise posting time from the relative age marker.

The website shows the same waiting window

The other supplied image shows BrickLink's maintenance page. The earlier recovery artwork has been replaced with a blue LEGO parrot wearing a yellow construction helmet. Under the heading “Temporarily unavailable,” the notice gives the same essential message: the site is offline while work is carried out, with unavailability expected until at least 6 p.m. CET / 9 a.m. PST.

Our fresh check of BrickLink's main website redirected to the official recovery page. The maintenance-page text matched the substance of the supplied website image. That supports the status reported at the time of this check. A screenshot on its own cannot tell us whether a service changes later in the day.

There is one useful difference between the two notices: the website wording shown in the image does not print a date, while the Instagram Story explicitly says “Nov 6.” Together, the images make the announcement easier to understand. They document what BrickLink was telling its community through its website and social account, rather than leaving the date to be inferred from discussion elsewhere.

“At least” is the important part of the time

The listed times refer to the same moment on November 6, 2026:

  • 9:00 a.m. Pacific Standard Time
  • 12:00 noon Eastern Standard Time
  • 5:00 p.m. UTC / GMT
  • 6:00 p.m. Central European Time

BrickLink says it expects the site to remain unavailable until at least that point. That is an earliest stated window, not a guaranteed reopening appointment. If the work takes longer, the notice's wording already leaves room for the interruption to continue beyond those times.

For a buyer, it means there is no sound basis for promising that checkout will work at noon Eastern. For a seller, it means a packing or shipping plan should not depend entirely on the site returning at that exact minute. The next meaningful development will be either a new official statement or a working marketplace that users can actually verify.

What the update answers, and what it does not

The two notices answer three immediate questions. BrickLink acknowledges that the site is unavailable. It says its teams are working on it. And the Instagram Story ties the earliest stated window to November 6. That is more specific than a general recovery screen asking people to wait.

The notices do not explain the underlying technical problem. “Necessary work” is the company's description, but it is not a detailed incident report. Neither supplied image establishes whether the work was planned in advance, what triggered it, or which systems require attention. We should not turn that short phrase into a more specific explanation that BrickLink has not given.

They also do not establish that data has been lost, that accounts have been compromised, or that every order is unaffected. Those are separate questions requiring separate evidence. An outage is a reason to check records carefully when access returns, not proof of a particular failure behind the scenes.

For the same reason, a maintenance page cannot confirm whether every support route is working. It is sensible to keep a record of a problem and any message already sent, but this update does not claim that support email has stopped operating or that a response will arrive within a particular time.

What buyers can do while they wait

If you were placing an order when access stopped, keep the records you already have. An order confirmation, payment receipt, and screenshot of the last page or error will be more useful than trying to reconstruct the sequence later.

  • Do not assume a missing page means an order failed. Compare confirmation emails, payment records, and the account's order history once you can reach it again.
  • Avoid paying twice. If a payment or checkout attempt is uncertain, resolve the first attempt before repeating it.
  • Keep the details together. Save the order number, seller name, approximate time, and exact error when available. Never include passwords or full payment-card details in a support message.
  • Allow for communication delays. A seller may be facing the same access problem. The maintenance notice does not by itself mean the seller has ignored an order.

If you are simply building a wanted list or planning a project, save any notes you can access outside BrickLink. There is no need to treat a temporarily unreachable list as evidence that it has disappeared. Wait for access to return, then check the actual list before rebuilding work from scratch.

What sellers should keep track of

For sellers, the disruption can interrupt several pieces of one workflow: checking an order, picking parts, updating stock, sending a message, and recording a shipment. Keeping those steps distinct makes it easier to reconcile work later.

Preserve existing inventory exports and order emails. If you pack an order or make a stock adjustment offline, note exactly what you did. A short, clear list of completed work and pending changes is safer than relying on memory when the site becomes available again.

Before repeating an upload, synchronization, or batch update, compare the saved records with the restored account. Something that appeared to stop halfway may require checking rather than rerunning immediately. This is precautionary workflow advice; it is not a report that BrickLink has duplicated or lost inventory.

If a customer needs an update, stick to what is known about their order and the official interruption. Avoid promising a dispatch time based solely on the earliest reopening window. The notices give a waiting estimate, not a guarantee about when every store's normal work can resume.

What will count as a meaningful recovery update?

A changed picture or a reachable homepage is not the whole test. Buyers need to be able to reach the relevant store and check their order status. Sellers need access to the records and tools required for their next step. A website can respond with a maintenance page while its usual marketplace remains unavailable.

Once access returns, check the work that matters to your account before repeating anything that may already have gone through. Review orders and payment status, compare inventory changes, and confirm queued work deliberately. If one page opens but another still fails, describe the specific result instead of assuming everything has recovered.

For now, the clearest development is the statement in the two images: BrickLink says it is carrying out necessary work and expects the interruption to last until at least 9 a.m. PST / 6 p.m. CET on November 6. The Instagram Story supplies the date, and the website notice gives the same waiting window. That is the update we can document. A full explanation and a confirmed return to normal service are still the next answers buyers and sellers need.
